title: Sphere Encoder 2

paper.title: Sphere Encoder 2
paper.abstract:
Abstract Sphere Encoder is an autoencoder that generates images by decoding random points from a high-dimensional latent sphere.
We identify two limitations of the original formulation that reduce its generation quality.
First, random points concentrate near the equator relative to the pole on an encoded latent, but the training rotation never reaches this region, leaving a gap that limits one-step generation.
Second, training for generation with pixel-wise reconstruction loss encourages the decoder to average over plausible images, producing blurry images that lack high-frequency details.
We present Sphere Encoder 2 to address both limitations, substantially improving image generation quality while maintaining the speed and simplicity of a autoencoder.
Models are released at github.com/kaiyuyue/sphere2 .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Sphere Encoders ( Yue et al., 2026 ; Do et al., 2026 ; Man et al., 2026 ) are simple standalone autoencoders with strong generative capabilities. They consist of an encoder that maps images into a spherical latent space, and a decoder that maps a latent vector back to an image. When trained properly, the training images cover the latent sphere with an approximately uniform distribution, enabling generation of novel images by sampling a random latent vector and passing it through the decoder. Unlike the many-step generation process used by diffusion models, sphere encoders enable fast image generation in as little as one step. The original Sphere Encoder ( Yue et al., 2026 ) is able to represent the ImageNet distribution, but its single-step generations are blurry ( Fig. 2 , top). Sharp images were obtained by iteratively passing a generated image through the encoder and decoder as many as 4 times, yet soft edges remain even after this refinement. We trace this to two causes. First, while noise is added to latent vectors during training to achieve good coverage of the sphere, the original Sphere Encoder only adds up to 85 ∘ 85^{\circ} of noise to latents, possibly leaving some of the sphere unseen during training. Second, it trains the decoder for generation with the pixel-wise reconstruction loss, which is minimized by averaging over all plausible images and thus yields blurry outputs. Sphere Encoder 2 fixes both issues ( Fig. 2 , bottom). First, we adopt a parameterization of noise that robustly adds a full 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} of noise to latents during training, allowing the decoder to see more of the sphere during training. Second, we decouple the decoder’s task into two regimes: low-noise reconstruction, which keeps the pixel-wise loss, and high-noise generation, which drops it. In the high-noise/generative regime, we propose a new and efficient latent score matching loss. This encourages outputs to lie on the image manifold without requiring adversarial training. The result is sharp one-step generation on ImageNet 512 × 512 512\times 512 ( Fig. 1 ). Among pixel-space generators on ImageNet, Sphere Encoder 2 achieves the best FDr 6 at 256 × 256 256\times 256 and the second best at 512 × 512 512\times 512 with only 4 × 2 4\times 2 network evaluations (NFE), whereas pixel diffusion models such as JiT ( Li & He, 2026 ) and PixNerd ( Wang et al., 2026a ) take 200. This amounts to 23 × 23\times to 40 × 40\times less sampling compute in total GFLOPs. Without classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , 4 steps outperform JiT-H and one-step pMF-H ( Lu et al., 2026 ) at both resolutions.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Autoencoders ( Bourlard & Kamp, 1988 ; Hinton & Zemel, 1993 ; Kingma & Welling, 2014 ) compress images into a latent space, but making them generate on their own is hard on complex datasets, e.g. , ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) . Hierarchical VAEs such as NVAE ( Vahdat & Kautz, 2020 ) and VDVAE ( Child, 2021 ) deepen the latent space, yet their generation quality stays far below diffusion models ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ) and GANs ( Sauer et al., 2023 ) . Deep VAEs ( Luhman & Luhman, 2023 ) reach high fidelity on ImageNet only when trained inside the latent space of a pretrained tokenizer. Autoencoders then settled for the two-stage paradigm: an autoencoder only compresses, and a secondary latent diffusion Rombach et al. (2022) or autoregressive (AR) prior ( Tian et al., 2024 ) generates. Sphere Encoder ( Yue et al., 2026 ) revisits single-stage paradigm with a non-variational autoencoder and reaches competitive quality on ImageNet, but its generation is blurry because it treats generation as reconstruction. Sphere Encoder 2 still stays single-stage but removes the blur. Sampling from a prior is what turns an autoencoder into a generator, and most work focuses on learning a richer prior, from mixture priors ( Tomczak & Welling, 2018 ) to the hierarchical priors above. Spherical latents have also been explored, but either at small scale with a von Mises-Fisher posterior ( Davidson et al., 2018 ) , or with a prior still learned on top of spherical latents, autoregressive in SphereAR ( Ke & Xue, 2025 ) and Riemannian flow matching over representation-encoder latents in RJF ( Kumar & Patel, 2026 ) . Sphere Latent Encoder ( Do et al., 2026 ) builds on Sphere Encoder without a learned prior, but it is two-stage again and relies on a RAE decoder ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) to reach pixels. StyleGAN ( Karras et al., 2019 ) normalizes its input noise onto a sphere, but it does not synthesize from the sphere directly: a learned mapping network first transforms random inputs into the intermediate latent space 𝒲 \mathcal{W} , whose distribution is also a learned prior. Closest to our setting, ( Zhao et al., 2019 ) decode random points on a sphere directly to pixels, but only working on MNIST and CelebA. Sphere Encoder is the first to scale sphere-to-pixel decoding to ImageNet: the decoder is trained with noise to cover the entire sphere, so no learned prior is needed. One-step and few-step generation can be reached by two main paths. Distillation compresses a pretrained multi-step teacher into a few steps, by progressively halving steps ( Salimans & Ho, 2022 ; Meng et al., 2023 ; Luhman & Luhman, 2021 ) , straightening trajectories ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , enforcing consistency ( Song et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) , or matching scores or distributions ( Luo et al., 2023b ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , optionally with an adversarial term ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) , while from-scratch methods train one/few-step models directly, including consistency training ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song & Dhariwal, 2024 ; Geng et al., 2025b ; Lu & Song, 2025 ; Luo et al., 2023a ) , flow-map methods such as shortcut models, IMM, MeanFlow and its variants ( Frans et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025a ; Geng et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Boffi et al., 2024 ) , drifting models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , GANs ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ; Brock et al., 2019 ; Kang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Sauer et al., 2023 ; Hyun et al., 2026 ) , and Sphere Encoders ( Yue et al., 2026 ; Do et al., 2026 ; Man et al., 2026 ) . Sphere Encoder 2 is trained from scratch without distillation. One step decodes random points on the sphere directly into pixels, and each extra step loops the model by encoding, rotating, and decoding. Distribution matching is the core of generative modeling for high-fidelity synthesis. The most effective method is the adversarial loss: a discriminator learns to tell real images from generated ones, and its gradient pushes the generator toward the data distribution ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ; Brock et al., 2019 ; Kang et al., 2023 ) . However, adversarial training needs careful tuning and architecture design ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Hyun et al., 2026 ) , and its stability is a problem: BigGAN ( Brock et al., 2019 ) collapses after a few hundred ImageNet epochs and must be stopped early, and the discriminator overfits as training proceeds ( Karras et al., 2020 ) . Distribution matching distillation (DMD) ( Yin et al., 2024b ) proposes an alternative: a pretrained diffusion teacher provides the real score, a second model tracks the fake score online, and their difference moves samples toward the data distribution ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . The cost is the teacher: DMD requires a pretrained diffusion model of the same data or a superset of it, so it is a distillation method rather than a standalone loss for any generator. SMT ( Jayashankar et al., 2025 ) tries to drop the teacher by learning the score of the real/fake mixture online, but operates in pixel space at 64 × 64 64\times 64 or below. Concurrent work matches real and generated features of frozen encoders with MMD or optimal transport ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , estimating the transport direction non-parametrically from a batch, but so far only as post-training of pretrained multi-step generators. In this work, we propose a lightweight score matching loss without a pretrained teacher. It trains two score models online from scratch, one for real and one for fake features, each a two-layer transformer following standard EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , and both operate in a frozen feature space rather than pixel space, as in Projected GAN ( Sauer et al., 2021 ) , StyleGAN-T ( Sauer et al., 2023 ) , and drifting loss ( Deng et al., 2026 ) . Like a GAN loss, the score matching loss depends only on real and generated images, not on the generator itself, so in principle it can be plugged into any generator training pipeline.

sections.heading: 3.1 Gap to the Equator
sections.text: For the direct pixel generation in Eq. 2 to succeed, the decoder must handle latents that are far from any encoded 𝐳 \mathbf{z} seen at training time. Sphere Encoder bridges the gap between the discrete training distribution and continuous uniform distribution using a process called spherify with noise , which adds noise to a clean latent 𝐳 \mathbf{z} before train-time reconstruction: 𝐳 ^ ​ ( α ) = ℱ ⁡ ( 𝐳 + tan ⁡ ( α ) ​ ℱ ​ ( 𝐞 ) ) , \displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{z}}(\alpha)=\mathcal{F}\left(\mathbf{z}+\tan(\alpha)\ \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{e})\right), (3) where α \alpha approximates the angle between 𝐳 \mathbf{z} and 𝐳 ^ ​ ( α ) \hat{\mathbf{z}}(\alpha) in high dimensions. During training, α \alpha is uniformly sampled from [ 0 , α max ] [0,\alpha_{\mathrm{max}}] with α max = 85 ∘ \alpha_{\mathrm{max}}=85^{\circ} . This objective leaves a mismatch between the latents seen in training and those used for generation. Specifically, on a high-dimensional sphere, almost all of the surface measure concentrates in a thin band around the equator relative to any fixed direction ( Blum et al., 2020 ; Goldstein & Studer, 2018 ) . Relative to 𝐳 \mathbf{z} , a random point ℱ ⁡ ( 𝐞 ) \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{e}) lies near the equator at α → 90 ∘ \alpha\rightarrow 90^{\circ} . With α max = 85 ∘ \alpha_{\mathrm{max}}=85^{\circ} , the decoder is never trained on the equatorial band, and the residual gap of 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} limits its one-step generation quality. Closing the gap by setting α max = 90 ∘ \alpha_{\mathrm{max}}=90^{\circ} is not an option in Eq. 3 , since tan ⁡ ( α ) \tan(\alpha) diverges as α → 90 ∘ \alpha\rightarrow 90^{\circ} . This main limitation motivates a new formulation that reaches the equator exactly.

sections.heading: 4.4 Taming the Generation Regime
sections.text: Reconstruction has been well studied in prior work ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Esser et al., 2024 ; Yue et al., 2026 ) , and is not the focus of this work. We keep the reconstruction regime as is, without adversarial sharpening, so that any change in generation quality can be attributed to the generation losses alone. Our focus in this work is the generation regime, with the goal set above: along the rotation arc in Fig. 3 , generated images should stay semantically consistent with the reconstruction while varying in appearance and structure.

sections.heading: 4.4.2 Fidelity Improvement
sections.text: Improving synthesis fidelity with a loss is a long-standing problem in generative modeling. The adversarial loss ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ; Brock et al., 2019 ; Kang et al., 2023 ) remains the most effective approach, but it requires careful tuning and architecture design ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Hyun et al., 2026 ) , and its long training suffers from stability issues ( Karras et al., 2020 ) . We seek a simple alternative with two properties: (1) it is stable over long training on large datasets, e.g. , hundreds of epochs on ImageNet; and (2) it consistently yields effective fidelity supervision as the generator improves, rather than saturating once the generator catches up. Inspired by DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Deng et al., 2026 ) , we propose a score matching loss that is agnostic to the generator and plugs in as a standalone loss module, in the same way as a GAN loss. Figure 7: Score matching loss. Fake features from the frozen extractor ϕ \phi are denoised by the real and fake score models (each a two-layer transformer EDM denoiser ( Karras et al., 2022 ) ), and their difference gives the direction 𝐠 \mathbf{g} that pulls fake features toward real ones. During transport, both score models are frozen and run once each; only the decoder 𝒟 \mathcal{D} is updated by 𝐠 \mathbf{g} through ℒ score \mathcal{L}_{\text{score}} . Like a GAN loss, it trains an auxiliary model online alongside the generator, but instead of a discriminator that classifies real from fake, it trains two lightweight score models, each only two transformer layers following standard EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , that estimate the real and fake distributions in a frozen feature space; their difference gives the direction to move fake features toward real ones. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Sphere Encoders are an emerging paradigm with progress from several teams ( Do et al., 2026 ; Man et al., 2026 ) , generating images with few steps and low compute. Sphere Encoder 2 takes this paradigm a step further, matching the image quality of more expensive diffusion models while keeping that simplicity and speed. It closes the gap to the equator with an explicit rotation, and splits the rotation arc into reconstruction and generation regimes on the same sphere. The generation regime is trained with a simple objective: semantic alignment and latent consistency keep generated images semantically faithful to the input but structurally different, and a lightweight score matching loss sharpens them without adversarial training. Several other families also targeted one-step generation from scratch, including consistency models, MeanFlow and its variants, drifting models, and GANs. Sphere Encoder 2 adds a complementary path to this landscape by bringing the autoencoder back as a generator in its own right and could be a viable candidate for one/few-step generation. sections.heading: B.1 Distribution Shift
sections.text: ℒ score \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{score}} matches the fake and real distributions in one feature space, ConvNeXt V2-N. As Sec. 5 notes, the match carries over to the five modern spaces of FDr 6 but not to the old Inception space of gFID, where the statistics of generated images drift away from those of real images. This is a mirror image of the metric paradox in FDr 6 ( Yang et al., 2026 ) : most generators beat gFID but not the eye, while ours satisfies the modern feature spaces but not gFID. Ideally, we could learn a feature space specific to ImageNet as drifting models do ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , or add score models in the Inception space, but both are expensive and cumbersome. We seek a simple and cheap alternative. To pin the statistics in place, we borrow an idea from FD loss ( Yang et al., 2026 ) and add a Fréchet distance term on frozen features as a regularizer: ℒ FD ​ - ​ lite = ∑ i FD ϕ i ​ ( 𝐗 ^ , 𝐗 ) sg ⁡ ( FD ϕ i ​ ( 𝐗 ^ , 𝐗 ) ) + ϵ , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FD\text{-}lite}}=\sum_{i}\frac{\ \mathrm{FD}_{\phi_{i}}(\hat{\mathbf{X}},\mathbf{X})\phantom{2}}{\phantom{1}\mathrm{sg}\big(\mathrm{FD}_{\phi_{i}}(\hat{\mathbf{X}},\mathbf{X})\big)+\epsilon}, (A15) where ϵ = 10 − 6 \epsilon=10^{-6} and FD ϕ i \mathrm{FD}_{\phi_{i}} is the Fréchet distance ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) between real and generated features from the i th i^{\mathrm{th}} frozen extractor ϕ i \phi_{i} . Each term is normalized by its own detached value, so every extractor contributes a gradient of unit scale. The mean and covariance of real and fake features are tracked with exponential moving averages (EMA) online, and FD ϕ i \mathrm{FD}_{\phi_{i}} is computed between them. We use three small extractors: Inception, our encoder ℰ \mathcal{E} (DINOv3-small, 29M), and our score feature extractor ϕ \phi (ConvNeXt V2-N, 16M). The latter two are already run for ℒ lat ​ - ​ con \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{lat\text{-}con}} and ℒ score \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{score}} , so ℒ FD ​ - ​ lite \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FD\text{-}lite}} adds one Inception forward and almost no compute. If a model is judged by human preference or prompt-following benchmarks rather than gFID, as text-to-image models commonly are, we believe ℒ FD ​ - ​ lite \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FD\text{-}lite}} is unnecessary and can be dropped. Relation to FD loss. We call ours ℒ FD ​ - ​ lite \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FD\text{-}lite}} because it differs from the original FD loss ( Yang et al., 2026 ) in purpose, and as a result in cost. The original is a post-training objective: it is the only loss applied to a pretrained multi-step generator, and its job is to repurpose the generator for one-step generation, which visibly and dramatically improves one-step quality. Ours is a regularizer. It runs alongside our other three losses throughout training with a small weight of 0.1 0.1 , and only keeps the statistics of already plausible samples from drifting particularly in the Inception space. Being a regularizer rather than the main objective, it does not need the heavy extractors of the original, Inception, SigLIP-so400M and MAE-Large, and reuses the two we already run in our loss functions. sections.heading: B.3 Angle Distribution in Training
sections.text: Diffusion models commonly concentrate training samples in the high-noise region, via a noise-level ( Li & He, 2026 ) or timestep shift ( Esser et al., 2024 ) . Sphere Latent Encoder ( Do et al., 2026 ) likewise found that concentrating samples at high-angle noise improves generation. One might expect Sphere Encoder 2 to benefit from more training at high angles as well, especially since its decoder is conditioned on α \alpha . To test this expectation, we train a Sphere2-B on Oxford Flowers 256 × 256 256\times 256 and control the sampling density of α \alpha during training with a single parameter by drawing it from a rational curve: α = 90 ∘ ⋅ ( k + 1 ) ​ r k ​ r + 1 , r ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] , \displaystyle\alpha=90^{\circ}\cdot\frac{(k+1)\,r}{k\,r+1},\quad r\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1], (A16) where k > − 1 k>-1 sets the shape of the curve ( Fig. A20 left). Setting k = 0 k=0 gives uniform sampling. A positive k k concentrates samples near the equator, and a negative k k near the pole. Fig. A20 middle and right tell a different story from common practice. Uniform sampling ( k = 0 k=0 ) gives the best 1-step gFID, and the best FDr 6 at every step count. Concentrating samples near the equator ( k > 0 k>0 ) buys only a marginal gain in multi-step gFID at k = 5 k=5 . We attribute this to the angle cutoff: each regime already receives a loss tailored to it, so the decoder no longer needs an uneven sampling density to prioritize the generation. We therefore use uniform sampling by default, as the simplest and most effective choice. Figure A20: Angle distribution in training. Left: sampling curves of α \alpha for different k k . Middle and right: generation quality of Sphere2-B on Oxford Flowers 256 × 256 256\times 256 for each k k . Uniform sampling ( k = 0 k=0 ) is the best choice.

sections.heading: C.1 Differentiable Augmentation
sections.text: We apply differentiable augmentations ( Zhao et al., 2020 ) to the decoder output before it is passed to the frozen feature extractor ϕ \phi during score model training. The decoder produces images of size 256 × 256 256\times 256 or 512 × 512 512\times 512 , and we mainly investigate DINO-S/8 ( Caron et al., 2021 ) and ConvNeXt V2-N(ano) ( Woo et al., 2023 ) as the feature extractor. For DINO-S/8, instead of resizing the image to 224 × 224 224\times 224 , we interpolate the positional embedding to match the image size. We use two differentiable augmentations: horizontal flip with probability 0.5, and translation with probability 1.0. The translation ratio is 0.015625 0.015625 for both resolutions, i.e., up to 4 pixels at 256 × 256 256\times 256 and 8 pixels at 512 × 512 512\times 512 , with reflect padding. The translation smooths the patch boundaries. Since DINO-S/8 uses 8 × 8 8\times 8 patches, a shift of up to 4 or 8 pixels is half a patch at 256 × 256 256\times 256 and a full patch at 512 × 512 512\times 512 , so the extractor sees the generated image at every offset relative to its patch grid.

sections.heading: C.2 Feature Standardization
sections.text: Eq. 9 standardizes the output of each scored layer j j of ϕ \phi . Since the procedure is identical for every layer, we drop the index j j here. The raw feature ϕ ( 𝐗 ) ∈ L × C \phi(\mathbf{X})\in\real^{L\times C} has L L spatial locations (ConvNeXt V2-N) or tokens (DINO-S/8) and C C channels. EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) assumes the input has zero mean and standard deviation σ data = 0.5 \sigma_{\mathrm{data}}=0.5 , so we standardize the layer feature to this scale before it enters the score models. Given a global batch of B B real images, we compute the per-channel mean and second moment of the raw features, m = 1 B ​ L ∑ b = 1 B ∑ l = 1 L ϕ ( 𝐗 b ) l , M = 1 B ​ L ∑ b = 1 B ∑ l = 1 L ( ϕ ( 𝐗 b ) l ) 2 , m , M ∈ C , \displaystyle m=\frac{1}{BL}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\phi(\mathbf{X}_{b})^{l},\quad M=\frac{1}{BL}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\big(\phi(\mathbf{X}_{b})^{l}\big)^{2},\quad m,M\in\real^{C}, (A18) where b b indexes the batch and l l indexes the spatial locations or tokens. The two statistics are accumulated as a running average over the first 1000 training steps and then frozen. Since ϕ \phi is frozen, they converge quickly, and freezing them keeps the standardization fixed for the rest of training. They are estimated on real features only and applied to both real and fake features. This keeps the score models blind to the distribution difference between real and fake features, which is what the transport is meant to expose. The standardization statistics of Eq. 9 are then μ = m , s = σ feat σ data , σ feat = M − m 2 ∈ C , \displaystyle\mu=m,\qquad s=\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{feat}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}},\qquad\sigma_{\mathrm{feat}}=\sqrt{M-m^{2}}\in\real^{C}, (A19) so that 𝐯 = ( ϕ ⁡ ( 𝐗 ) − μ ) / s \mathbf{v}=(\phi(\mathbf{X})-\mu)/s has zero mean and standard deviation σ data \sigma_{\mathrm{data}} in every channel. For ConvNeXt V2-N, we keep s s per-channel wise, because a few channels have far larger variance than the rest. This is because the Global Response Normalization (GRN) layer leaves one channel dominating the others in magnitude. Each channel’s standard deviation is floored at 0.1 0.1 times the median over channels, so a nearly constant channel is not amplified. For DINO-S/8, the channels are naturally balanced, and we use a single scalar s s per layer, the root mean of the per-channel variances.

We identify two limitations of the original formulation that reduce its generation quality. First, random points concentrate near the equator relative to the pole on an encoded latent, but the training rotation never reaches this region, leaving a gap that limits one-step generation. Second, training for generation with pixel-wise reconstruction loss encourages the decoder to average over plausible images, producing blurry images that lack high-frequency details. We present Sphere Encoder 2 to address both limitations, substantially improving image generation quality while maintaining the speed and simplicity of a autoencoder. Models are released at github.com/kaiyuyue/sphere2 . Figure 1: Curated 1-step generation without CFG on ImageNet 512 × 512 512\times 512 by Sphere Encoder 2. Figure 2: Sphere Encoder vs. Sphere Encoder 2. Uncurated generation on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 from Sphere Encoder ( Yue et al., 2026 ) (top) and Sphere Encoder 2 (bottom) with same classes. 1 Introduction Sphere Encoders ( Yue et al., 2026 ; Do et al., 2026 ; Man et al., 2026 ) are simple standalone autoencoders with strong generative capabilities. They consist of an encoder that maps images into a spherical latent space, and a decoder that maps a latent vector back to an image. When trained properly, the training images cover the latent sphere with an approximately uniform distribution, enabling generation of novel images by sampling a random latent vector and passing it through the decoder. Unlike the many-step generation process used by diffusion models, sphere encoders enable fast image generation in as little as one step. The original Sphere Encoder ( Yue et al., 2026 ) is able to represent the ImageNet distribution, but its single-step generations are blurry ( Fig. 2 , top). Sharp images were obtained by iteratively passing a generated image through the encoder and decoder as many as 4 times, yet soft edges remain even after this refinement. We trace this to two causes. First, while noise is added to latent vectors during training to achieve good coverage of the sphere, the original Sphere Encoder only adds up to 85 ∘ 85^{\circ} of noise to latents, possibly leaving some of the sphere unseen during training. Second, it trains the decoder for generation with the pixel-wise reconstruction loss, which is minimized by averaging over all plausible images and thus yields blurry outputs. Sphere Encoder 2 fixes both issues ( Fig. 2 , bottom). First, we adopt a parameterization of noise that robustly adds a full 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} of noise to latents during training, allowing the decoder to see more of the sphere during training. Second, we decouple the decoder’s task into two regimes: low-noise reconstruction, which keeps the pixel-wise loss, and high-noise generation, which drops it. In the high-noise/generative regime, we propose a new and efficient latent score matching loss. This encourages outputs to lie on the image manifold without requiring adversarial training. The result is sharp one-step generation on ImageNet 512 × 512 512\times 512 ( Fig. 1 ). Among pixel-space generators on ImageNet, Sphere Encoder 2 achieves the best FDr 6 at 256 × 256 256\times 256 and the second best at 512 × 512 512\times 512 with only 4 × 2 4\times 2 network evaluations (NFE), whereas pixel diffusion models such as JiT ( Li & He, 2026 ) and PixNerd ( Wang et al., 2026a ) take 200. This amounts to 23 × 23\times to 40 × 40\times less sampling compute in total GFLOPs. Without classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , 4 steps outperform JiT-H and one-step pMF-H ( Lu et al., 2026 ) at both resolutions. 2 Related Work Autoencoders ( Bourlard & Kamp, 1988 ; Hinton & Zemel, 1993 ; Kingma & Welling, 2014 ) compress images into a latent space, but making them generate on their own is hard on complex datasets, e.g. , ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) . Hierarchical VAEs such as NVAE ( Vahdat & Kautz, 2020 ) and VDVAE ( Child, 2021 ) deepen the latent space, yet their generation quality stays far below diffusion models ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ) and GANs ( Sauer et al., 2023 ) . Deep VAEs ( Luhman & Luhman, 2023 ) reach high fidelity on ImageNet only when trained inside the latent space of a pretrained tokenizer. Autoencoders then settled for the two-stage paradigm: an autoencoder only compresses, and a secondary latent diffusion Rombach et al. (2022) or autoregressive (AR) prior ( Tian et al., 2024 ) generates. Sphere Encoder ( Yue et al., 2026 ) revisits single-stage paradigm with a non-variational autoencoder and reaches competitive quality on ImageNet, but its generation is blurry because it treats generation as reconstruction. Sphere Encoder 2 still stays single-stage but removes the blur. Sampling from a prior is what turns an autoencoder into a generator, and most work focuses on learning a richer prior, from mixture priors ( Tomczak & Welling, 2018 ) to the hierarchical priors above. Spherical latents have also been explored, but either at small scale with a von Mises-Fisher posterior ( Davidson et al., 2018 ) , or with a prior still learned on top of spherical latents, autoregressive in SphereAR ( Ke & Xue, 2025 ) and Riemannian flow matching over representation-encoder latents in RJF ( Kumar & Patel, 2026 ) . Sphere Latent Encoder ( Do et al., 2026 ) builds on Sphere Encoder without a learned prior, but it is two-stage again and relies on a RAE decoder ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) to reach pixels. StyleGAN ( Karras et al., 2019 ) normalizes its input noise onto a sphere, but it does not synthesize from the sphere directly: a learned mapping network first transforms random inputs into the intermediate latent space 𝒲 \mathcal{W} , whose distribution is also a learned prior. Closest to our setting, ( Zhao et al., 2019 ) decode random points on a sphere directly to pixels, but only working on MNIST and CelebA. Sphere Encoder is the first to scale sphere-to-pixel decoding to ImageNet: the decoder is trained with noise to cover the entire sphere, so no learned prior is needed. One-step and few-step generation can be reached by two main paths. Distillation compresses a pretrained multi-step teacher into a few steps, by progressively halving steps ( Salimans & Ho, 2022 ; Meng et al., 2023 ; Luhman & Luhman, 2021 ) , straightening trajectories ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , enforcing consistency ( Song et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) , or matching scores or distributions ( Luo et al., 2023b ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , optionally with an adversarial term ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) , while from-scratch methods train one/few-step models directly, including consistency training ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song & Dhariwal, 2024 ; Geng et al., 2025b ; Lu & Song, 2025 ; Luo et al., 2023a ) , flow-map methods such as shortcut models, IMM, MeanFlow and its variants ( Frans et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025a ; Geng et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Boffi et al., 2024 ) , drifting models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , GANs ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ; Brock et al., 2019 ; Kang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Sauer et al., 2023 ; Hyun et al., 2026 ) , and Sphere Encoders ( Yue et al., 2026 ; Do et al., 2026 ; Man et al., 2026 ) . Sphere Encoder 2 is trained from scratch without distillation. One step decodes random points on the sphere directly into pixels, and each extra step loops the model by encoding, rotating, and decoding. Distribution matching is the core of generative modeling for high-fidelity synthesis. The most effective method is the adversarial loss: a discriminator learns to tell real images from generated ones, and its gradient pushes the generator toward the data distribution ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ; Brock et al., 2019 ; Kang et al., 2023 ) . However, adversarial training needs careful tuning and architecture design ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Hyun et al., 2026 ) , and its stability is a problem: BigGAN ( Brock et al., 2019 ) collapses after a few hundred ImageNet epochs and must be stopped early, and the discriminator overfits as training proceeds ( Karras et al., 2020 ) . Distribution matching distillation (DMD) ( Yin et al., 2024b ) proposes an alternative: a pretrained diffusion teacher provides the real score, a second model tracks the fake score online, and their difference moves samples toward the data distribution ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . The cost is the teacher: DMD requires a pretrained diffusion model of the same data or a superset of it, so it is a distillation method rather than a standalone loss for any generator. SMT ( Jayashankar et al., 2025 ) tries to drop the teacher by learning the score of the real/fake mixture online, but operates in pixel space at 64 × 64 64\times 64 or below. Concurrent work matches real and generated features of frozen encoders with MMD or optimal transport ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , estimating the transport direction non-parametrically from a batch, but so far only as post-training of pretrained multi-step generators. In this work, we propose a lightweight score matching loss without a pretrained teacher. It trains two score models online from scratch, one for real and one for fake features, each a two-layer transformer following standard EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , and both operate in a frozen feature space rather than pixel space, as in Projected GAN ( Sauer et al., 2021 ) , StyleGAN-T ( Sauer et al., 2023 ) , and drifting loss ( Deng et al., 2026 ) . Like a GAN loss, the score matching loss depends only on real and generated images, not on the generator itself, so in principle it can be plugged into any generator training pipeline. 3 Preliminaries: Sphere Encoder Sphere Encoder ( Yue et al., 2026 ) is a non-variational autoencoder that can be efficiently sampled to generate images. We address this next. 4.4.2 Fidelity Improvement Improving synthesis fidelity with a loss is a long-standing problem in generative modeling. The adversarial loss ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ; Brock et al., 2019 ; Kang et al., 2023 ) remains the most effective approach, but it requires careful tuning and architecture design ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Hyun et al., 2026 ) , and its long training suffers from stability issues ( Karras et al., 2020 ) . We seek a simple alternative with two properties: (1) it is stable over long training on large datasets, e.g. , hundreds of epochs on ImageNet; and (2) it consistently yields effective fidelity supervision as the generator improves, rather than saturating once the generator catches up. Inspired by DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Deng et al., 2026 ) , we propose a score matching loss that is agnostic to the generator and plugs in as a standalone loss module, in the same way as a GAN loss.
